title: briefing_ai_on_brand_voice
claim: AI models generate generic copy because teams feed them style adjectives instead of negative operational rules.

evidence.detail: A prompt engineering test for corporate comms: replace tone adjectives with explicit negative constraints and forbidden industry cliches.

slides.headline: Adjectives produce average text
slides.body: Tone adjectives pull the web statistical average. You end up with generic corporate filler.

slides.headline: Define what the model cannot say
slides.body: Models follow boundaries better than mood words. When briefing AI on brand voice, ban specific terms.

items.label: Ban buzzwords
items.detail: Zero instances of game-changer or unlock

slides.headline: Swap tone guidelines for constraints
slides.body: Replace style guides with operational limits. Give the model hard stops instead of open-ended descriptors.

items.label: Hard Constraint
items.detail: Max 18 words per line. No questions.

slides.headline: Run the generic copy test
slides.body: If output works for a competitor by swapping names, your prompt constraints failed.

items.label: Competitor Swap
items.detail: Fails if text fits rival unchanged

items.label: Evidence Check
items.detail: Requires one spec, standard, or figure

slides.headline: The four prompt boundary rules
slides.body: Add these four rules to your custom instructions before generating public comms.

items.label: Rule 2
items.detail: No unbacked claims of quality or speed

items.label: Rule 3
items.detail: Use active verbs and short sentences

items.label: Rule 4
items.detail: State the tradeoff when naming a feature

slides.headline: Rules shape voice better than adjectives
slides.body: Brand voice is not created by asking for personality. It is enforced by setting strict limits on output.

slides.headline: Precision comes from exclusion.
slides.body: Send this to whoever is writing your team's AI prompt guidelines this week.

caption:
Adjectives ruin your AI prompts.

When briefing AI on brand voice, most teams copy and paste their marketing style guide: "make it bold, authoritative, and human." Then they wonder why the output sounds like every other enterprise software brochure written in the last two years.

Language models treat tone adjectives as statistical weighted averages. Asking for "innovative" simply pulls the most common, generic phrases associated with innovation across the web.

If you want custom output, stop describing the vibe. Start writing negative constraints. Tell the model what it is explicitly forbidden to say, which words to ban, and what sentence structures to avoid.

Setting boundaries shapes writing faster than asking for personality.

Send this to whoever is building your team's custom prompts this quarter.
